summaries.example: Imagine a friend drops a stack of books. Hume would ask what feelings arise when someone helps: we may approve of kindness because it is pleasing and useful. Kant would ask whether helping is a duty we could expect everyone to follow, and whether we are respecting the friend as a person rather than treating them like a tool.
summaries.summary: This entry compares two famous thinkers, David Hume and Immanuel Kant. Hume explains morality by looking at human nature and feelings. We approve of traits such as kindness or fairness when they are useful, pleasant, or helpful to people. Sympathy helps us consider others instead of judging only from our own private likes and dislikes. Kant gives morality a different foundation. He says reason gives us duties that bind every rational person, even when following them is difficult or conflicts with a desire. His idea of autonomy means that a rational person can give herself a moral law and guide her choices by it. Kant’s categorical imperative asks us to choose rules we could accept as rules for everyone and to treat people as ends, never merely as tools. The philosophers also disagree about virtue, freedom, and religion. Hume sees freedom as being able to act from one’s own motives without force. Kant thinks deeper freedom involves a will that can be guided by moral reason. Both value morality and freedom, but they explain their foundations in very different ways.
key_ideas: Hume says morality grows from human feelings, especially approval, disapproval, sympathy, and concern for usefulness or pleasure.
Kant says morality is mainly about duties that reason gives us and that apply unconditionally.
Both philosophers think virtue matters, but Hume connects virtue with traits people approve of, while Kant connects it with strength in following moral duty.
Hume and Kant both separate morality from religion, though Kant gives religion a closer supporting role than Hume does.
They both think freedom matters for morality, but Hume focuses on acting from one’s own motives, while Kant focuses on whether the will can follow reason.
summaries.why_it_matters: These ideas help us notice two important sides of ethical life. Feelings such as sympathy can help us understand people and care about their happiness. Rules and duties can remind us to be fair even when we do not feel like it. Comparing Hume and Kant shows why people can agree that an action matters while disagreeing about what makes it right.

important_terms.definition: Rules about what people should do and how they should treat one another.
A strong feeling of approval or disapproval that helps Hume explain moral judgments.
Kant’s idea that a person’s will can guide itself by a moral rule instead of simply obeying outside pressure or desire.
Kant’s highest moral command: a rule that applies to every rational person, not just when it is convenient.
The good habits or qualities that help someone live and act well.
The ability to act according to one’s own will rather than being forced by someone else.
The belief that every event has causes. Hume says this can still fit with freedom when actions come from a person’s own motives.

questions_to_think_about: Is an action good because it helps people, because people approve of it, because it follows a rule, or for more than one reason?
Can someone be free if their choices have causes?
Should feelings help us decide what is right?
Can a person do the right thing for the wrong reason?

summaries.example: Suppose a student discovers that a close friend cheated on an exam. Hume’s approach asks which motives and character traits are being displayed, and how a well-informed, impartial observer would respond. Honesty and concern for fairness may win approval because they support social trust and are useful to others. Kant’s approach asks whether the student’s maxim—perhaps “I may hide cheating when a friend benefits”—could be willed as a universal rule, and whether hiding it would treat other students merely as means. Kant also stresses that applying a principle requires judgment about the concrete situation, not mechanical rule-following.
summaries.summary: The entry examines how Hume and Kant offer rival but partly connected approaches to morality. Hume’s naturalistic project explains moral life through human psychology. Moral evaluation begins with sentiments of approval and disapproval directed toward motives and character traits. Reason helps us understand consequences and social arrangements, but sentiment supplies moral valence. Sympathy and the general point of view correct merely personal reactions, allowing qualities such as justice, generosity, and prudence to be assessed in relation to human welfare and social life. Kant instead treats duty, obligation, and moral law as central. The categorical imperative expresses an unconditional demand of practical reason. Its formulations include testing whether a maxim could be universal law and requiring that humanity always be treated as an end, never merely as a means. Kant’s mature rejection of sentimentalism is directed at its inability, in his view, to ground a law that binds all rational beings necessarily and universally. Still, Kant does not eliminate feeling from ethics: respect may connect reason with motivation, and sympathy and emotional sensitivity assist moral judgment and the cultivation of virtue. Their accounts of virtue and freedom reveal the same contrast. Hume defines virtue through the responses of a judicious spectator, while Kant defines it as strength in ordering inclination beneath moral law. Hume reconciles freedom with causal necessity by identifying freedom with unforced action arising from the agent’s motives. Kant distinguishes the empirical standpoint from the standpoint of rational freedom and holds that morality presupposes a will capable of being determined by reason. key_ideas: The deepest disagreement concerns morality’s foundation: Hume locates it in human nature and sentiment, whereas Kant locates it in practical reason and the autonomy of rational agents.

Hume treats reason as useful for discovering facts and means, but not as the ultimate source of motivation or moral approval. Kant argues that pure reason can determine the will, although human moral judgment also needs experience, emotional sensitivity, and judgment.

For Hume, virtues are traits that a judicious spectator approves, often because they are useful or agreeable. For Kant, virtue is moral strength: the cultivated capacity to follow duty despite competing inclinations.

Hume’s freedom is compatible with causation because an action is free when it flows from the agent’s motives rather than force. Kant’s account looks upstream to the determination of the will and connects freedom with rational self-legislation.

Both reject the idea that morality must be founded on religion. Hume emphasizes religion’s possible distortion of moral judgment, while Kant argues that moral commitment can support a rational need to believe in God without making morality depend on divine commands.

Kant’s mature ethics rejects sentimentalism as the foundation of unconditional obligation, but feelings such as respect, sympathy, conscience, and compassion still matter in human motivation and in applying moral principles.
summaries.why_it_matters: The comparison clarifies several enduring questions: whether morality is discovered through human emotional life or generated by rational principles; whether consequences, motives, or universal rules deserve priority; and what kind of freedom responsibility requires. It also cautions against a simple opposition between reason and emotion. Hume gives reason an important instrumental role, while Kant’s mature view still needs feeling and experience for human moral agency. Studying both theories therefore helps explain why ethical disagreement can concern not only particular answers, but also what counts as a proper foundation for answering moral questions.

important_terms.definition: A view that moral evaluation is grounded chiefly in human sentiments, such as approval, disapproval, and sympathy.
Kant’s view that the will is self-legislating and self-directing under moral reason, rather than determined by external authority or inclination alone.
A command that binds unconditionally, independently of a person’s desires or chosen goals.
A practical principle describing what an agent intends to do; Kant tests whether such principles can be universalized.
Hume’s perspective of a suitably informed and disinterested observer whose sympathy broadens private reactions into moral evaluation.
The view that freedom and causal determination are compatible. Hume identifies freedom with action proceeding from one’s own motives rather than external compulsion.
Kant’s distinction between the empirical world, where events are governed by causal laws, and the intelligible standpoint from which rational agency can be regarded as free.
A moral quality that Kant associates with acting from duty, while Hume instead emphasizes the natural motives behind virtuous conduct.

questions_to_think_about: Can an empirical account of how people approve and disapprove explain what they ought to do, or does Kant’s distinction between facts and obligations require a different foundation?
Does acting from duty have greater moral worth than acting from sympathy, gratitude, or affection?
Is Hume’s freedom from external compulsion sufficient for responsibility, or must a responsible agent possess Kantian rational freedom?
Can a moral theory treat justice as a socially developed virtue, as Hume does, while also giving it universal authority?
Does Kant’s moral argument for belief in God establish knowledge, belief, or only a practical commitment?

summaries.example: A student sees a new student eating alone at lunch. Hume might say that welcoming the student is a virtue because kindness and friendliness usually create approval and help people live together. We should not decide only from personal jealousy or dislike; we should try to view the situation fairly and sympathetically. Kant might ask whether the rule “Ignore people when including them is inconvenient” could be a rule for everyone. He would also ask whether the lonely student is being respected as a person, not treated as someone unimportant.
summaries.summary: The entry compares David Hume’s and Immanuel Kant’s theories of morality. Hume explains ethics by studying human beings as natural and social creatures. We approve of motives and character traits that are useful or pleasing, especially when we judge from a fair-minded point of view and use sympathy to understand how actions affect others. Hume therefore gives feelings the leading role in moral evaluation, while reason helps us learn facts and consequences. Kant argues that morality cannot rest only on changing human feelings. Feelings differ among people and could have been different, so they cannot explain a law that binds every rational person. For Kant, reason gives us duties that apply whether or not we want to follow them. His categorical imperative asks us to choose principles that could be universal rules and to respect humanity in every person. Kant’s view does not make emotions useless. Respect, sympathy, conscience, and emotional awareness can help human beings carry out and apply moral duties. The philosophers also disagree about virtue. Hume sees it as a quality that earns approval, while Kant sees it as moral strength shown in choosing duty over temptation. On freedom, Hume is a compatibilist: caused actions can still be free when they come from the person rather than from force. Kant is concerned with whether the will itself can be guided by reason. Both thinkers make morality independent of religion, though Kant gives religion a role connected with the moral hope for a highest good.
key_ideas: Hume and Kant both think morality needs a foundation, but Hume looks to human nature while Kant looks to rational agency.
Hume says moral approval is connected to useful or agreeable qualities and is shaped by sympathy and a fair-minded point of view.
Kant says moral requirements are unconditional. A choice is morally acceptable only if its guiding rule can fit with a universal moral law.
Hume sees virtue mainly in admired traits and motives; Kant sees virtue as the strength to follow duty when desires pull in another direction.
Both connect morality with freedom, but Hume emphasizes freedom from force and Kant emphasizes freedom of the will.
Both separate morality from religion, although Kant thinks moral reasoning can give people a reason to hold religious beliefs.
summaries.why_it_matters: Hume and Kant offer two powerful ways to think about everyday choices. Hume reminds us that moral life involves sympathy, relationships, and the effects of character on people. Kant reminds us that fairness should not disappear when feelings change and that people must not be used merely for someone else’s benefit. Their disagreement helps us ask not just “What should I do?” but also “What makes an answer genuinely moral?”

important_terms.definition: The study of what makes actions, motives, and character good or bad, and what people ought to do.
The view that feelings, rather than reason alone, are central to moral judgment.
A character quality or habit that tends to be admired or approved, such as generosity or honesty.
A requirement about what someone must or must not do.
Kant’s idea that a person can guide herself by a moral law she recognizes through reason, rather than by outside orders or changing wants.
A rule that commands everyone, no matter what they happen to want or what goal they have.
Hume’s fair-minded perspective: judging motives with sympathy rather than from private advantage alone.
The view that freedom can exist even when actions have causes, as long as a person is not forced and acts from her own motives.

questions_to_think_about: Would an action still be right if nobody praised it?
Is following a rule enough, or do a person’s motives matter too?
Can feelings such as sympathy improve moral decisions, or can they make decisions unfair?
What is the difference between being unforced and being truly self-directed?
Why might philosophers think morality should not depend on religion?
